title: Grit Fest 2026: When The Homies F*ck With The Vision – Spencer Harding
content:
In 2026, Austin Killips took the helm of the Bentonville-based nonprofit All Bikes Welcome. With only a few months to prepare, she scrambled the homies from all parts of her bike life to come together and make the “first annual 6th Grit Fest” happen. Austin invited Spencer to check out what happens when the homies fuck with the vision…

Now you might be thinking, “That is a lot of cussing for an inclusive nonprofit’s yearly bike gathering”, and you would be right, but it was a phrase Austin kept relaying to me over and over throughout my week in Arkansas, so let’s run with it.

Want to throw a silly scavenger hunt…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Want to have a drag king roll in on an electric Tostitos scooter and dazzle attendees with jawlines and rose petals alike…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Want to raise money to open a non-profit bike shop in Fayetteville…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Need to screen print merch on thrifted clothing in your front yard…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Want to host a group of deaf cyclists so they can attend MTB clinics…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

When your event coordinator slips a disk in their back the day before the event… that’s right…call the homies who fuck with the vision.

Welcome

I had never attended any previous Grit Fest events due to being a cis male identifying person, as the previous iterations were focused on catering toward femme, trans, and non-binary folks. I understand my place in the bike world and the very real desire for many events to focus on non-cis male attendees, as most bike events are heavily male-dominated. Hell, the first question I asked Austin when she invited me to come document the event was, “Can I come to Grit Fest?” She retorted that she planned to do something totally new with Grit Fest and, as the nonprofit moniker says, All Bikes Welcome. Trusting Austin wholeheartedly, I booked my ticket.

Our backdrop for the weekend would be Lake Leatherwood, about an hour’s drive from the Bentoville/Fayettevile area. Nestled in a low valley with trail systems on either side of the lake and a quick jaunt from Eureka Springs. The North side of the lake is dominated by the Lake Leatherwood Bike Park, a part of the OZ trail system, while the south side of the lake has less gravity-focused trails.

Friday evening featured a chill ride led by Ian Henrikson, who will be helming the future Fayetteville bike shop. We found that even a chill ride to the top of the Leatherwood trails was no easy feat. The berms and rocky sections of Shreddy Yeti gave a glimpse of the potential of the trail system. A quick downhill had us making our way to camp to make sure we didn’t miss the 6 pm keynote speech. The Keynote featured Austin from All Bikes Welcome, Bird from Wheel Mouse, and Biscuit from Cyclocross For Everyone. The talk outlined the vision for the weekend’s event and moving forward with All Bikes Welcome and how the new version of Grit Fest came together.

While I didn’t get a recording of the Keynote, I did ping Austin for an interview post-event of her talking points:

Why Did You (Austin And Team) Have To Build A Different Event?

Well, I can say that the shift was not at all my intention or expectation when I stepped into this role. I don’t think it is useful to get into the weeds, but the grant and funding landscape that sustained many inclusion initiatives across and well beyond our industry has disappeared or been reallocated to other projects.

For Grit [Fest] to exist in the coming years, we had to shift to being self-sustaining instead of an event underwritten by grant funding. So we took it upon ourselves to build an event that shares the same moral foundation and outcome goal of an inclusive and welcoming space for beginners and people underrepresented in the world of bikes, but embraced a different collection of design principles.

In our “keynote address,” we talked about the imperative of building grassroots events as foils to the seeming bubble economy of these large corporate events that so often feel like they’re built for everyone and no-one. Words like “grassroots” and “community” get lobbed around with reckless abandon by people who, for lack of a better phrase, like likes. My framework for a grassroots event is something realized by the participants. I think you can embed that in the structure and design of an event in many ways, but something very important to me and my collaborators in Chicago with Cyclocross For Everyone is distributing the means of event production.

If we want to continue building a healthy and self-sustaining event ecosystem outside of entities like USAC and Lifetime, attendees need to leave feeling both held by the space we built over the course of the event and empowered to go build something with their friends back home.

What Challenges Did You Face?

Oh gosh, well, there were a lot of challenges, Spencer. Have you organized an event like this before? I have not; it turns out they are really complicated objects, made more unwieldy when you have about six months to make it happen and less than half of the historical budget.

I think the biggest challenge came the week of the event. Our event coordinator, Bronwen, slipped a disc and was in the hospital with some serious complications, and the park manager of our venue was also out with the flu. Losing the two people that were involved in all of the planning meetings meant I was constantly managing the micro and macro of the event. But, watching our cohort of volunteers and friends come together to make everything run smoothly was this beautiful collective exercise. It was really beautiful to see this motley crew of longtime supporters and new friends of the org rally together to make an event happen.

Organizing an accessible event for our disabled friends at the event was also a totally new challenge for me. I feel like I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about non-sighted users and participants over the last few years, and this is obviously the inverse of that. We are fortunate to have Ciara Logan, a local deaf mountain biker and activist involved with All Bikes Welcome, to help us steer the programming and accessibility services on-site. I think we did a solid job this year, but I’m really excited to collaborate with our deaf attendees for 2027 on signing resources for all event attendees, optimizing the lighting so our interpreters aren’t bathed in moody shadows at key moments, and scavenger hunt challenges that explicitly encourage building connections across the language gap.

What Do You Hope To Create Looking Toward Next Year’s Event?

I want to fill Lake Leatherwood with weirdos on the margins: people who range from being bike curious to local rippers, but who largely share this experience of not quite feeling a sense of place at a lot of bike events. The scavenger hunt is a really fun way to build something with a low skill floor and a high skill ceiling for participants because it’s unwinnable and simply encourages you to go frolic and find a balance between pedaling and being creative.

I’m also excited to keep playing with all the silly performance art stuff. Eureka Springs is an island unto itself, but Northwest Arkansas is America’s neoliberal test kitchen, and I think it’s ripe for a ribbing. Next year will be our founders summit. Expect lanyards, a slide deck presented on a slide projector, a full update on our annual KPI’s, CSF’s, EBITDA’s, Q3 numbers, and more pencil skirts. Our success is your success.

Oh, I also want to host single-speed cyclocross worlds.

Is This The gayest Bike Event Of The Year?

I’m retired from competing in things, but I do think we made a very gay and transgender bike event. We had furries in our midst, a medley of genders, and a drag show. We’re not competing, but we could certainly be in the running.

I do think it’s important to build spaces for the folks who have been explicitly shunted out of this sport. If It’s not governing bodies banning us, it’s coordinated campaigns on the internet disseminating our likenesses to millions of cruel ghouls on the internet chasing any opportunity to draw blood. Even if we’re not barred from participation, trans people still have to ask whether lining up is worth the psychic wound of potentially being featured on the homepage of a right-wing tabloid. I hope we can become a space for some of the people who have lost a sense of place in the ecosystem of events that courted us and our money for years and then promptly caved to astroturfed social pressures orchestrated by organizations invested in making the world a worse place and perpetuated by people with corroded souls.

A Gritty Saturday

Saturday morning came quickly, and I found myself devouring baked goods from Shady Grove Farm Bakery and chasing them with some good ol’ Camp Coffee. The first half of the day was devoted to bike clinics, ranging from first touch all the way up to advanced skills. I joined the advanced class because I wanted to work on my jumps and drops since both are in short supply back home in Tucson. The ever-featured Leatherwood Bike Park had a plethora of man-made features for the group to sample and get rowdy on. I likewise wanted to be present to document a cadre of deaf cyclists who joined in the clinic. All Bikes Welcome hired two interpreters for the weekend to make sure the deaf cyclists could participate and keep up with all the activities. It was a logistical lift to get the interpreters way up on the MTB trails, but many thanks to our liaison from the Lake Leatherwood who…you guessed it…fucked with the vision.

The afternoon was filled with workshops, talks, and people scrambling around to complete their scavenger hunt manifests. I had a lovely conversation with Jen from the Mendery, a local Fayetteville gear mending business, which I plan to visit next time I’m in town. I picked up a fancy new bowl from Dark Horse Pottery, whose proprietor, Allison, was part of the team helping to screen print merch before the event. After plinking some cans with a slingshot, as the scavenger hunt called for, and a trip to walk along the lake, it was time for dinner. A plethora of platters and falafel filled the large table as everyone dug in.

Tostitos, an Electric Scooter Cooler, and a Schwinn Signed by Courtney Cox

Just before dinner, our entertainment for the evening arrived: Dr. J Maniac, who rolled in on an electric scooter/cooler, our drag king for the night. After everyone had eaten, the Dr. included, we formed a long line of chairs for Dr. Maniac’s performance. After a tambourine-and rose-petal-filled performance of Celine Dion’s classic “It’s All Coming Back to Me Now,” the raffle commenced.

As you can see, the prize table was stacked! Austin had to cut people off after they’d won two prizes. I was able to trade a shoulder bag and bar tape I’d won for the box of, personally, much-coveted magic cards! When a non-nerd won the Warhammer set, they graciously donated it to our chef for the weekend, who held up the massive box and proclaimed “FOR THE EMPIRE.” Everything wound up right where it needed to be.

Even the Grit Fest men’s, women’s, and non-binary winners were chosen by raffle in addition to the sprinter and climber awards. Anyone could win! Chicago did somehow sweep the top three spots of Grit Fest, maybe some raffle interference…

Once all the prizes, including a bike frame from Chumba, were dolled out, karaoke began. Thanks to Smith, most folks got to wear their sunglasses at night; their futures were looking way too bright…

Biscuit was nearly falling out of their chair laughing about the prospect of explaining to someone that our chef was singing “Not Over You” on a grass stage with a Tostitos electric scooter cooler and a Schwinn signed by Courtney Cox. This moment has never happened before and will never be recreated…

Holy Water Hardstyle

Sunday morning was likewise filled with a menagerie of baked goods washed down with Camp Coffee and a hearty platter of pancakes. Grit Fest offered up two ride options for the day: a 15 and 30 mile ride option. The 15 mile was mainly gravel and pavement with a small helping of single track, while the 30 had a larger helping of single track and a visit to nearby Eureka Springs. Having heard much about the lore of Eureka Springs over the past few days, I elected to try the longer ride, if only to see the famous Eureka Springs. With a toss of the sacrificial Specialized Vita, we were off…

An equally steep uphill and downhill brought our crew to our first aid station courtesy of the Gnargo folks. Camp Coffee had crafted coffee-freezy pops for the riders, which were an instant hit. As we got closer to Eureka Springs, I spied more pride flags and an equal amount of Jesus-y messaging. As we reached one of the famous springs near town, Thomas was nice enough to bless everyone as they took a drink from the healing spring. As we wound our way through the Passion Play trails, we eventually pedaled our way to the iconic Christ of the Ozarks. After paying our respects with wheelies and hardstyles, we hit the trails to get back to Leatherwood.

Our group mulled around until our last wayward companion, Kaitlyn, finished the whole 30 mile loop that most of us had cut short. We welcomed her back with a proper friend tunnel to close out the weekend. Caitlin was the only true finisher of Grit Fest 2026, praise be.

This year’s Grit Fest was a testament to what can be created in short order when you have a devoted group of homies you can call on to make shit happen, and happen it did. I left the weekend with a full heart and a bunch of new friends from all over. I am excited to see Austin keep up this amazing energy with some proper time to prepare and the subsequent bike shop in Fayetteville.

If you are looking at these photos and thinking, “I fuck with the vision,” keep your eyes peeled for Grit Fest 2027; I have zero doubts it’ll be a banger.
